title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 163-165): Euler seeks a relation between x and y with y(0)=0 and y(a)=p, y(b)=q, y(c)=r, ... He takes y/x to be even in x and writes down its Lagrange interpolant in the variable x^2 (Cor. 3, p.165). Applied to y = sin x and evaluated at x=0, where sin x/x = 1, this gives 1 = Σ_k (sin a_k / a_k) Π_{j≠k} a_j^2/(a_j^2 - a_k^2). If the arcs a_k are known rational multiples of π, this yields π.

This page (end of §11): take four arcs Φ, 2Φ, 3Φ, 4Φ. The Lagrange weights are Π_{j≠k} j^2/(j^2-k^2):
- k=1: 8/5;
- k=2: -4/5;
- k=3: 8/35;
- k=4: -1/35.
Hence Φ ≈ (8/5) sinΦ - (2/5) sin2Φ + (8/105) sin3Φ - (1/140) sin4Φ.

In modern terms this is polynomial (Neville/Richardson-type) extrapolation to h=0, in powers of h^2, of g(h) = sin h / h from the samples h = Φ, 2Φ, 3Φ, 4Φ. Equivalently it extrapolates the inscribed-polygon semiperimeters N sin(π/N) when Φ = π/n. The truncation error is O(Φ^8).

Euler's two test values:
- Φ = π/2: π/2 ≈ 8/5 - 8/105 = 32/21, so π ≈ 3 1/21 ≈ 3.048.
- Φ = π/6 (sines of 30°, 60°, 90°, 120° only): π ≈ 184/35 - 171√3/140 ≈ 3.141567. The error is about 2.6×10^-5, matching Euler's 'aliquot particulis centies millesimis'.

§12 (Exemplum I, solved on p.167): take infinitely many arcs kΦ. The weights become Π_{j≠k} j^2/(j^2-k^2) = 2(-1)^{k+1}; Euler states 'all these products have value 2' without proof. The result is Φ/2 = Σ (-1)^{k+1} sin kΦ / k. Special cases:
- Φ = π/2 gives the Leibniz series.
- Φ = π/4 gives 1 + 1/3 - 1/5 - 1/7 + ... = π/(2√2).
- Φ = π/3 gives 1 - 1/2 + 1/4 - 1/5 + ... = π/(3√3).

With infinitely many equally spaced nodes, Π_j (1 - x^2/(j^2Φ^2)) = sin(πx/Φ)/(πx/Φ). Euler's general formula of p.165 is then exactly the (symmetric) Whittaker-Kotelnikov-Shannon cardinal series. His identity is the cardinal-series reconstruction of sin x at x→0. It holds precisely for |Φ| < π, i.e. sampling spacing below the Nyquist spacing for frequency 1. Euler meets the failure at Φ = π in §16 and explains it away by a limiting argument.
errors: No mathematical errors found. All four Lagrange weights, the value 32/21, the closed form 184/35 - 171√3/140 and the error claim (~2.6e-5) check out.

Gap (p.167): the claim that every infinite product Π_{j≠k} j^2/(j^2-k^2) equals 2 (more precisely 2(-1)^{k+1} with the alternating signs absorbed) is asserted without proof. It is true, following from the sine product.
Gap: the validity range |Φ| < π of the infinite-node identity is not stated on this page. It is only addressed, unsatisfactorily, in §16.

ideas.what: Evaluating at x=0 the Lagrange interpolant in x^2 of sin x / x through nodes Φ,...,4Φ, as a quadrature-free approximation of π.
ideas.modern_name: Polynomial (Richardson/Neville) extrapolation to the limit in h^2; Romberg-type acceleration of Archimedes' polygon method
ideas.usually_credited_to: Huygens 1654 (first step only); Richardson 1910/1927 ('deferred approach to the limit'); Romberg 1955
ideas.where_published: This paper E555 (Opuscula analytica I, 1783). I am unsure whether histories of extrapolation (e.g. Brezinski's surveys, Joyce 1971) cite it.

ideas.what: Explicit numerical value π ≈ 184/35 - 171√3/140 from sines of 30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, accurate to ~3e-5.
ideas.usually_credited_to: unsure; I know of no attribution
ideas.where_published: E555 only, as far as I know

ideas.what: Infinite-node Lagrange interpolation with equally spaced nodes, giving Φ/2 = Σ(-1)^{k+1} sin kΦ / k.
ideas.modern_name: Cardinal (Whittaker-Shannon) interpolation series; Fourier series of the sawtooth
ideas.usually_credited_to: The Fourier series to Euler himself (1744 letter to Goldbach; E246, 1755). The cardinal series to Cauchy 1841 / Borel 1897 / E.T. Whittaker 1915 / Kotelnikov / Shannon.
ideas.where_published: The series in E246 and Institutiones calculi differentialis. The interpolation derivation in E555.

missed.claim: Euler performs a genuine multi-point polynomial extrapolation to zero in h^2 (three Richardson steps), not just Huygens' single step. He uses the arithmetic node sequence Φ, 2Φ, 3Φ, 4Φ, gives explicit weights, and obtains π to ~3e-5 from elementary sine values. He also notes that accuracy improves as Φ decreases. This is a clear pre-Richardson instance of 'deferred approach to the limit' that standard extrapolation histories do not seem to credit.
missed.quote: Φ = 8/5 sin.Φ - 2/5 sin.2Φ + 8/105 sin.3Φ - 1/140 sin.4Φ ... π = 184/35 - 171√3/140, qui valor tantum aliquot particulis centies millesimis a vero differt
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It belongs in the prehistory of Richardson/Romberg extrapolation, between Huygens (1654) and Saigey/Richardson, and shows Euler viewed Lagrange interpolation at the limit point as a convergence-acceleration device.

missed.claim: With nodes kΦ (k = 1, 2, ...), Euler's interpolation formula is exactly the cardinal (Whittaker-Shannon) series in symmetric form. His derived identity Φ/2 = Σ(-1)^{k+1} sin kΦ/k is valid exactly when the sample spacing Φ < π, i.e. below the Nyquist spacing for sin x. The breakdown at Φ = π that he discusses in §16 is aliasing at the Nyquist rate. Euler did not draw this link, and I do not know of sampling-theory histories citing E555.
missed.quote: Progrediantur arcus a, b, c, d, etc. secundum seriem numerorum naturalium ... ex quorum sinibus p, q, r, s, etc. veram longitudinem arcus Φ determinari oporteat
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It would place an explicit equally-spaced infinite-node sampling reconstruction, together with a worked example of the Nyquist threshold, in Euler (1783), well before Cauchy/Borel/Whittaker.

deep.surprise_reason: The interpolation-to-zero computation of π is an explicit, correct multi-step Richardson-type extrapolation with a striking numerical result, likely unnoticed in histories of extrapolation. The infinite-node version is a cardinal series exhibiting the Nyquist condition. Both are plausible but unverified gaps in the record; the series themselves are well known.
transcription_corrections: No substantive errors found in the transcription of p.166. Formulas match the image: weights 8/5, -2/5, 8/105, -1/140, π/2 = 8/5 - 8/105 = 32/21, π = 3 1/21, π = 184/35 - 171√3/140.
p.167 3°: the series π/6 = √3/2 - (1/2)(√3/2) * + (1/4)(√3/2) - (1/5)(√3/2) + ... is consistent with sin values at multiples of 60°. The '*' marks the vanishing term sin 3Φ.
p.167 'omnia autem haec producta eundem reperiuntur habere valorem = 2' refers to absolute value; the alternating signs are carried by the leading ± in each row.
